title: MB5-03826
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), is appealing against the August 13, 2015, decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) to reject her claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), is appealing against the August 13, 2015, decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) to reject her claim for refugee protection. She is asking the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to allow the appeal, set aside the RPD's determination and substitute its own determination or refer the matter to the RPD for re-determination by a differently constituted panel.
The appellant did not present any new evidence pursuant to subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and is not requesting that a hearing be held before the RAD.
The Minister did not intervene in this appeal, but did intervene by submitting documents before the RPD.

Pursuant to subsection 111(1) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD, namely, that the appellant is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA or a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of section 97 of the IRPA.
The appeal is dismissed.

In her Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), the appellant alleges that she has been a member of the opposition party Union pour la démocratie et le progrès social (UDPS) [union for democracy and social progress] since December 2009. Her involvement in the UDPS allegedly consisted of participating in meetings and raising awareness among women in her district. In December 2011, she allegedly participated in a demonstration against the presidential election results. At this event, she was supposedly stopped and arrested, then mistreated by the Congolese police forces. She was allegedly detained and, even though he could have been penalized, a guard officer released her on December 11, 2011.

The appellant also alleges that she received a summons to appear that, in her initial BOC Form, was dated February 26, 2012, but was amended at the hearing before the RPD to December 28, 2011. During her appearance, the appellant was apparently questioned. She was prohibited from any further involvement with the UDPS, and she was allowed to leave a few hours later. Subsequently, the appellant left the DRC on May 27, 2012, for Canada, using a visitor's visa. Then, in August 2012, men in uniform allegedly went to her house looking for her. After their visit, members of her family who lived with her allegedly fled to another area. She was supposedly informed by neighbours that men in uniform were lurking on her street.

In its August 13, 2015, decision, the RPD rejected the claim for refugee protection. The RPD's findings can be summarized as follows: - Several issues were raised in relation to the appellant's credibility, including the following: (a) The RPD did not believe that the appellant went to hide in the municipality of Kisenso beginning on December 11, 2011, as she claims, given the contradiction with respect to the address indicated on the relevant immigration form and the lack of any indication to this effect in her BOC Form. (b) There are contractions related to the date of the appellant's appearance at the offices of the Congolese authorities. (c) There is an implausibility, namely, that the appellant allegedly went to the Congolese authorities on January 6, 2012, that she was released illegally and that she hid from the authorities in the municipality of Kisenso as of December 11, 2011. (d) There is an implausibility, in the context of the DRC, namely, that the appellant would have received nothing more than a reprimand from the Congolese authorities had she fled from detention; (e) There are inconsistencies arising from the appellant's inability to state why the authorities of her country were looking for her and to state the specific date on which her problems with the authorities began. (f) There are inconsistencies and contradictions in the appellant's testimony, arising from an arrest warrant submitted as evidence, dated January 5, 2012, and it is implausible that the appellant was released on January 6, 2012, when she had not responded to a previous summons, and that this matter was not discussed during her alleged appearance on January 6, 2012. (g) Given these inconsistencies and contradictions, the RPD gave no weight to the documents submitted to support her alleged problems. (h) It is not plausible that the appellant was able to leave the DRC without difficulty, if she was being sought by the authorities. (i) For all these reasons, the RPD did not believe that the appellant was being pursued by the Congolese authorities, that she was detained in December 2011, or that she was released in the alleged circumstances. (j) Also, the appellant's behaviour is inconsistent with that of a person who fears returning to their country, given that the appellant waited more than 35 months after coming to Canada to claim refugee protection and that her explanations were considered unreasonable, especially since the appellant has been here without legal status since May 2014. (k) Although the RPD found that the appellant had established that she was a member of the UDPS and although it took into account the documentary evidence, it found that the appellant had not established a serious possibility of persecution and that, on a balance of probabilities, she would not be personally subjected to a risk to her life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture, should she return to the DRC.

In the appellant's memorandum, in addition to the arguments about the standard of review that the RAD must use, arguments that I will address later in my reasons, the appellant's lawyer claims that the RPD committed errors that can be summarized as follows: - The RPD based its findings on factors that are irrelevant and non-determinative. The RPD also failed to clearly establish the factors relevant to this matter and the weight to be given to them, as well as how it concluded that the male appellant would not be subjected to a risk of persecution, should she return to the DRC. - For these reasons, the RPD's decision lacks consistency and intelligibility. - Also, the RPD erred in the assessment of the facts and failed to consider all the evidence brought before it.
The appellant's lawyer claims that the RPD made unreasonable errors that require the RAD to intervene.
I find that the scope of the RAD appeal must be examined in light of the IRPA and the case law on this subject.
First, the IRPA does not explicitly state the standard of intervention that the RAD must apply when it reviews RPD decisions.

In addition, with respect to RAD decisions, subsection 111(1) of the IRPA states that the RAD shall confirm the determination of the RPD, set aside the determination and substitute a determination that, in its opinion, should have been made, or refer the matter to the RPD for re-determination, giving the directions to the RPD that it considers appropriate.

In Huruglica, the Federal Court of Appeal found that the role of the RAD is to intervene when the RPD is wrong in law, in fact or in fact and law.1 It also found that an appeal before the RAD is not a true de novo proceeding.2 And it clearly set out the approach that the RAD must take: [103] I conclude from my statutory analysis that with respect to findings of fact (and mixed fact and law) such as the one involved here, which raised no issue of credibility of oral evidence, the RAD is to review RPD decisions applying the correctness standard. Thus, after carefully considering the RPD decision, the RAD carries out its own analysis of the record to determine whether, as submitted by the appellant, the RPD erred. Having done this, the RAD is to provide a final determination, either by confirming the RPD decision or setting it aside and substituting its own determination of the merits of the refugee claim. It is only when the RAD is of the opinion that it cannot provide such a final determination without hearing the oral evidence presented to the RPD that the matter can be referred back to the RPD for redetermination. No other interpretation of the relevant statutory provisions is reasonable.

With respect to the degree of restraint or deference owed by the RAD to the RPD's findings as to the credibility or value of any testimony, the Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica also states the following: [70] This also recognizes that there may be cases where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage over the RAD in making findings of fact or mixed fact and law, because they require an assessment of the credibility or weight to be given to the oral evidence it hears. It further indicates that although the RAD should sometimes exercise a degree of restraint before substituting its own determination, the issue of whether the circumstances warrant such restraint ought to be addressed on a case-by-case basis. In each case, the RAD ought to determine whether the RPD truly benefited from an advantageous position, and if so, whether the RAD can nevertheless make a final decision in respect of the refugee claim. [71] One can imagine many possible scenarios. For example, when the RPD finds a witness straightforward and credible, there is no issue of credibility per se. This will also be the case when the RAD is able to reach a conclusion on the claim, relying on the RPD's findings of fact regarding the relative weight of testimonies and their credibility or lack thereof. [72] Problems will occur when the credibility findings themselves are disputed on appeal, and the RAD has no way to reach a conclusion without endorsing or rejecting those findings. If the RAD can identify an error in situations where, for example, a claimant was not found credible because his story was not plausible based on common sense, the RPD may have no real advantage over the RAD. [73] Similarly, there may also be cases where a finding that a witness is not credible was based on discrepancies that could not justify such a conclusion or that simply did not exist. If the assessment of the oral evidence contains an error which the RAD can easily identify, but the weight to be given to this testimony is essential to determine whether the RPD decision should be confirmed or set aside, the RAD may conclude that it is a proper case to refer back to the RPD with specific directions in respect of the error identified in the credibility findings. [74] That said, it is not appropriate to say more about the various scenarios that may arise, for they are not before us. The RAD should be given the opportunity to develop its own jurisprudence in that respect; there is thus no need for me to pigeon-hole the RAD to the level of deference owed in each case.

Thus, it is my opinion that the RAD is a specialized tribunal and that I must conduct an independent assessment of all the evidence to determine whether the appellant is a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA or a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of section 97 of the IRPA, and therefore, whether the RPD's decision is well founded in light of the evidence presented to the RPD, the appeal record, as well as any new evidence within the meaning of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, or any evidence gathered during a hearing under subsection 110(6) of the IRPA, if applicable. In the case at hand, it should be noted that the appellant did not present any new evidence and there was no hearing before the RAD.

In examining this case, I will show a measure of deference to the RPD's findings in terms of the appellant's credibility, which are based on her testimony. Also, if there are errors on questions of law or if there are erroneous findings or findings not supported by the evidence on questions of fact or of mixed law and fact that are at the heart of essential elements of the refugee protection claim, I will intervene in accordance with the provisions of subsections 111(1) and 111(2) of the IRPA.

The determinative issue is whether the RPD erred in its decision. In examining the issue, I reviewed the RPD's reasons for decision and listened to the recording of the hearing before the RPD. I also read and analyzed all the evidence in this case, as well as the appellant's memorandum.

First I will address the findings regarding the appellant's credibility, including the one related to the appellant's behaviour that was considered inconsistent with that of a person who allegedly fears for their life, then the one related to the appellant's membership in the UDPS. RPD's credibility findings (a) Findings other than the one concerning the appellant's delay in claiming refugee protection in Canada

The RPD identified several inconsistencies and implausibilities surrounding the appellant's allegations. The appellant's lawyer argues that the findings are not based on determinative elements and that not only did the RPD err in its assessment of the facts, but it also failed to take into account all the evidence.
I do not agree with the appellant's lawyer's statements, for the reasons that follow.

To begin, the RPD accepted as evidence all the documents submitted by the appellant. As well, during the hearing the RPD asked questions about the reasons behind the refugee protection claim, including the documents submitted. Moreover, it is trite law3 that the RPD is presumed to have considered all the evidence before it and that it is not required to comment on every piece of evidence. For these reasons, I am of the opinion that the appellant's lawyer's statements are unfounded.

The appellant testified that she had been arrested on December 9, 2011, mistreated, then detained for two days. She was subsequently released by a police officer on December 11, 2011. Shortly after, she allegedly hid at the home of a cousin in the municipality of Kisenso (Kinshasa). When confronted with the address on the IMM-5669 immigration form,4 which appears to be unchanged from April 2009 until she left the DRC in May 2012, and which is not the Kisenso address, the appellant replied that it was the address of her family home in Kinshasa. When confronted with the lack of any reference in her BOC Form to the fact that she supposedly hid in Kisenso, she reiterated that she had lived in Kisenso.

Based on my analysis of all the evidence, I find it reasonable to believe that, had the appellant hidden for more than five months at the home of her cousin in Kisenso, she would have stated so in her BOC Form and in her immigration form, even though her home address was in another Kinshasa district, given the importance of this allegation and in order to support her allegations that she was hiding. I find that this alleged hiding is an essential element of the refugee protection claim and, like the RPD, I am of the opinion that she did not credibly establish that she hid in the alleged circumstances.

The appellant testified that a notice to appear had been issued on January 5, 2012, after her release. The appellant testified that it was her children who had come to see her to inform her of this notice to appear. She testified several times that she had appeared before the Congolese authorities on January 6, 2012. When asked by the RPD whether there had been contact with police authorities between December 11, 2011, the alleged day of her release, and January 6, 2012, the day of her appearance, the appellant answered no. Later at the hearing, when she was asked to explain the reasons for which her initial BOC Form mentions that the notice to appear had been received on February 26, 2012, she did not provide any explanations and she reiterated that it was on January 5, 2012. When confronted with the notice to appear5 that she had submitted, summoning her to appear on December 28, 2011, the appellant stated that she may have forgotten the date.

Like the RPD, I find that there are a number of inconsistencies/contradictions between the appellant's testimony and the documentary evidence. First, I find it reasonable to believe that if a notice to appear had been issued on December 28, 2011, the initial BOC Form would have reliably indicated this date, not the date of February 26, 2012, and the appellant would have been able to provide a reasonable explanation for this significant two-month discrepancy. In addition, the appellant testified before the RPD at least five times that she had appeared on January 6, 2012, the day after she allegedly received the notice to appear. I find that her testimony again contradicts the notice to appear and, in the circumstances, I find that the appellant's explanations, according to which she may have forgotten the date when she was confronted with the documentary evidence, are insufficient, especially since she testified that she had not had any contact with the police before the said appearance. This undermines the appellant's credibility on another essential element of her refugee protection claim, and I attach no probative value to the notice to appear submitted.

Also, when asked why the appellant had met with the police authorities, despite the fact that she was allegedly released illegally and she was in hiding, the appellant replied that she had no choice and that the police authorities were going to come back to the family home, when her children were living there. She added that she had gone there with a UDPS leader. She was allegedly prohibited from participating in UDPS activities and, after some hours spent at the police station, she left. The RPD found that there was an implausibility, namely, that the appellant went to the police authorities on January 6, 2012.

I considered the appellant's explanations. However, I find it reasonable to believe that, if the appellant feared the police authorities and she was in hiding in Kisenso, she would not have gone to the offices of the police authorities, even with a UDPS representative. Also, if this meeting had taken place and no sanction had been imposed on her by the authorities, and she had been allowed to leave, I do not find it credible that the appellant would have gone to hide again in order to avoid the police, since there was no indication that the police were interested in her. For these reasons, I find that the appellant failed to credibly establish this alleged meeting with the authorities.

The appellant was questioned by the RPD about an arrest warrant6 that she submitted as evidence. First, she testified that she did not know why it had been issued. She then added that it was issued after her meeting with the authorities. Confronted with the document itself, which is dated January 5, 2012, the appellant stated that it was issued when she was hiding in Kisenso.

Based on my analysis of the arrest warrant, it is dated January 5, 2012, and it states that it was issued because of the appellant's failure to respond to a summons to appear. Like the RPD, I find that there are inconsistencies in the appellant's testimony. First, the appellant referred to a notice to appear received the day before, which had been the reason for her visit to the authorities, not the arrest warrant. Second, how can it be that this arrest warrant came after a meeting on January 6, 2012, when it is dated prior to this meeting? Also, the appellant cannot explain the grounds of the arrest warrant and she did not testify that she had failed to appear in response to a notice she had allegedly received before. For all these reasons, I attach no probative value to the arrest warrant submitted.

The appellant testified that she was being sought by the DRC authorities, since the police went to her house in August 2012, which led her family members to leave the family home to go to Kisenso and, subsequently, that men in uniform were lurking in the area of the family home. The appellant submitted a wanted notice7 and letters8 to support her allegations. The RPD did not believe that the appellant was being sought, given the inconsistencies in the appellant's testimony and that it was not plausible that the appellant was being sought, when she had left the DRC without assistance from an intermediary and without any difficulties.

Based on my analysis of the recording of the hearing before the RPD, the appellant testified that she had not had any problems between January 6, 2012, and May 27, 2012, the day she left the DRC. Also, she clearly testified that there had been no sanctions by the police authorities, except that she was held at their office for a few hours. She also testified that she did not understand why they were looking for her. Based on my analysis of the letters submitted, the one dated August 22, 2012, is from the appellant's neighbour, informing her that the house is closed up because her family members are no longer there and that the house has been vandalized. There is no date of that visit. However, the letter dated August 25, 2012, is from one of the appellant's family members, informing her of the same visit by soldiers, still not specifying the date of this visit. She also specified, among other things, that UDPS documents belonging to the appellant were burned and that the soldiers allegedly stated that the appellant was a leader in the district.

Although I am of the opinion that the RPD's finding of implausibility with respect to the appellant's leaving the DRC is not sufficiently supported by the documentary evidence, it did not commit a determinative error to this effect, for the reasons that follow.

First, the RPD made findings on the credibility of several essential elements of the refugee protection claim, which were based on the oral and documentary evidence. Based on my previously stated findings, namely, that I did not find credible the appellant's allegations about the notice to appear which, according to the alleged facts, had been issued after her [translation] "illegal" release, or the allegations about her meeting with the authorities, or those about the arrest warrant, like the RPD, I do not find credible the appellant's allegations that were the source of the authorities' [translation] "interest" in the appellant, in this case her arrest, detention, mistreatment and release.

Since I did not believe the difficulties that the appellant alleged to have had with the Congolese authorities, I attach no probative value to the wanted notice or the letters9 submitted to support the allegations of searches conducted by DRC authorities. Moreover, the date of the alleged visit by soldiers is not specified in the previously mentioned letters. Also, it should be noted that, if the house was closed up and the appellant's family members were not there at the time of the soldiers' alleged visit, the letter of August 25, 2012, does not explain how the person who wrote the letter was informed of the visit. This letter also does not contain any explanations as to how the person who wrote it learned that the soldiers had burned UDPS documents belonging to the appellant, or that she was identified as a leader in the district. Furthermore, it should be noted that the August 22, 2012, letter from the neighbour does not contain these details. (b) Appellant's delay in claiming refugee protection in Canada

The appellant came to Canada on May 27, 2012, using a visitor's visa for which the date of expiry was extended at the time of her arrival, to May 26, 2014.10 The appellant filed a claim for refugee protection on April 10, 2015. She explained to the RPD that she had not claimed refugee protection or tried to regularize her status for the reasons that follow. First, she believed that her problems would be temporary and she wanted to return to the DRC, then she referred to her lack of information about how to make a claim for refugee protection. The RPD did not find these explanations satisfactory and it concluded that the appellant's behaviour was not consistent with that of a person who feared for their life, should they return to their country, and this reinforced its conclusion not to believe that the authorities were looking for her.

I agree with the RPD's findings, for the reasons that follow. First, like the RPD, I agree that, if the alleged fear of the Congolese authorities were true, the appellant would not have waited more than 35 months to regularize her situation, especially since she had been without legal status since May 26, 2014.

It should be noted that a number of Federal Court decisions have confirmed Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada decisions that concluded that having valid, but temporary, status did not constitute acceptable grounds for a delay in claiming refugee protection. For example, the Honourable Justice de Montigny states the following in Nijjer, Yadhwinder Singh:11 It is trite law that a delay in submitting a refugee protection claim, while not decisive, remains a relevant element that the tribunal may take into account in assessing both the statements and the actions and deeds of a claimant: Huerta v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) (1993), 157 N.R. 225 (F.C.A.), [1993] F.C.J. No. 271. The claimant knew upon his arrival in Canada that he was only authorized to stay in Canada for a specific and limited period of time. Under these circumstances, it was reasonable to expect that he would regularize his status as soon as possible if he truly feared for his life and physical integrity in India.

The appellant delayed claiming refugee protection in Canada, for nearly three years after she came to Canada. Although not determinative, this delay was a factor that the RPD could take into account in its decision. The RPD did not err in its finding that the appellant's behaviour undermined her credibility and that this reinforced its findings of non-credibility with respect to alleged searches for the appellant. RPD's findings about the appellant's membership in the UDPS

The RPD found that the appellant had established her membership in the UDPS. However, the RPD found that the appellant had failed to establish that she would be subjected to a reasonable chance of persecution, should she return to the DRC, under subsection 96 of the IRPA, or that she would be subjected to a risk set out in section 97 of the IRPA.
I agree with the RPD's findings, for the reasons that follow.

First, the documentary evidence12 refers to the fact that the UDPS, founded in 1982, is a legally recognized opposition party in the DRC, and the party participated in the presidential elections held in 2011. This same documentary evidence also refers to the fact that members of the opposition, including UDPS members, may be subjected to arrests and abuse by the Congolese authorities, particularly during mass activities protesting the Congolese government. In this respect, the documentary evidence13 indicates, among other things, that on December 9, 2011, and in the days that followed the announcement of the presidential election results, there were arrests and a human rights violation committed by the Congolese authorities against opposition members.

It is not illegal to be a UDPS member in the DRC. Although the documentary evidence indicates that people may have been arrested, mistreated and detained in relation to the presidential election held in 2011, given my previously mentioned findings, I have found that this was not the case for the appellant. For the same reasons, I have found that the appellant did not credibly establish that the Congolese authorities were interested in her. Although the appellant testified that she has been a member since December 2009, that she attended monthly UDPS meetings and that, by word of mouth, she shared information of interest with women in her district, there is no indication that she suffered any harm in connection with these activities. Given the circumstances of this case, although the appellant established her membership in the UDPS, since I did not believe her allegations regarding her detention, arrest and [translation] "illegal" release, or regarding the Congolese authorities' interest in her, she failed to establish the basis of her claim in light of sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA, should she return to the DRC.

After reviewing all the oral and documentary evidence, given the previously stated reasons and pursuant to subsection 111(1) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD, namely, that the appellant is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA or a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

The appeal of XXXX XXXX XXXX is dismissed. Louis Cousineau Me Louis Cousineau May 25, 2016 Date IRB translation Original language: French 1 Minister of Citizenship and Immigration v.
